lessons.title: The Wilting Maize of Kibwezi: Encountering the Phenomenon

quiz.prompt: A farmer in Kibwezi waters her maize early in the morning. By midday the leaves are drooping. Amina writes on her prompt card: "Plants only wilt when the soil is dry." Which fact from the story is hard to fit with Amina's idea?
choices: Maize near the dry seasonal riverbed wilts sooner
The maize wilted at midday even though the soil was watered that morning
Some plants stand upright again by evening
The sukuma wiki under the mango tree looks healthy all day
quiz.rationale: Amina's idea says wilting happens only when the soil is dry, but the maize wilted although the farmer had watered that morning. This is the tension the lesson wants students to notice. It is not yet explained.
quiz.placement: Predict: prompt card story, writing two things you think you already know and one question

quiz.prompt: Students look at a photograph of maize in a dry Kibwezi field at midday. They must write only what they can SEE, not an explanation. Which sentence is an observation?
choices: The maize is wilting because its roots cannot take in water
The maize leaves are curling inward and the soil around the plants looks damp
The maize will die because the farmer did not water enough
The maize is wilting because the midday sun has dried the plant out
quiz.rationale: Curled leaves and damp-looking soil can be seen directly in the photograph. The other choices are explanations or predictions, which belong in the "What It Makes Me Think" column.
quiz.placement: Observe: See-Think-Wonder observation sheet, column "What I See" for photograph A

quiz.prompt: In the Kibwezi scenario, a farmer compares maize growing near a dry seasonal riverbed with maize on a lower, wetter slope. Which observation matches what was shown?
choices: Both groups of maize wilted at the same time
Neither group of maize wilted, but the sukuma wiki did
Maize on the lower, wetter slope wilted sooner than maize near the riverbed
Maize near the dry riverbed wilted sooner and more severely than maize on the lower, wetter slope
quiz.rationale: Photograph B showed maize near the dry seasonal riverbed wilting more severely than maize on the lower, wetter slope. This is an observation only and does not yet explain why.
quiz.placement: Observe: photograph B, maize near the dry seasonal riverbed compared with maize on the lower, wetter slope

quiz.prompt: At this point in the unit, a student is asked: "Why might a maize plant wilt even when the soil around it has water?" Which response best fits where the class is after the Kibwezi photographs?
choices: It is because maize plants cannot take in any water from the soil
It has not been explained yet; we have first ideas and will investigate and test them in the coming lessons
It is because the soil water is used up by midday, so the farmer must water again
It is because the farmer did not water enough, so the question is already answered
quiz.rationale: This is the anchor lesson, so the phenomenon is left unexplained. Students record first ideas in their diagrams and notebooks and revisit them as the unit develops. The photographs show damp soil, so the other choices are not supported.
quiz.placement: Explain: group diagrams, gallery walk and individual first-draft explanation "I think the maize wilts because..."

quiz.prompt: The class is filling the Driving Question Board with two columns: "What We Think We Know" and "What We Wonder". Which sticky note belongs in the "What We Wonder" column?
choices: Sukuma wiki under a mango tree stays healthy
How does water get to the very top of a tall tree?
Plants need water to stay alive
Maize leaves droop in the afternoon in Kibwezi
quiz.rationale: A genuine question about something we want to find out belongs under "What We Wonder". The other three are statements the students think they already know or have seen.
quiz.placement: DQB: sticky notes posted in the columns What We Think We Know and What We Wonder

quiz.prompt: Students draw a first model of a maize plant (roots, stem, leaves). They put a question mark next to any part they are unsure about. Why?
choices: Because only students who already know everything are allowed to label parts
To show honestly what they are unsure about, so the model can be improved as they investigate in later lessons
So the teacher can mark the unsure parts wrong and take away marks
So they can rub those parts out and leave them blank for ever
quiz.rationale: Question marks make uncertainty visible and treat it as the starting point of investigation. The baseline model is not graded and will be updated at the end of every lesson.
quiz.placement: Model: starting the cumulative whole-plant model in the science notebook, marking unsure parts with a question mark

lessons.title: What Do Plants Need to Survive? — Mapping the Case for a Transport System

quiz.prompt: A Grade 10 class lists what a maize plant needs to stay alive and healthy. Which list contains the four essential needs of a plant?
choices: Sunlight, carbon dioxide, ready-made food and fertiliser only
Mineral salts, sugar from the soil, water and wind
Water, mineral salts, carbon dioxide and sunlight
Water, ready-made food from the soil, oxygen and shade
quiz.rationale: Plants need water, mineral salts, carbon dioxide and light energy. They make their own sugar in the leaves and do not take food from the soil.
quiz.placement: Journal prompt and think-pair-share: 'List everything a plant needs to stay alive' (board heading WHAT PLANTS NEED)

quiz.prompt: On a maize plant, where do the mineral salts that the plant needs enter the plant?
choices: Through the stem, from sunlight
Through the leaves, from the air
Through the roots, from the soil water
Through the flowers, from the rain
quiz.rationale: Mineral salts are dissolved in soil water and are taken in by the roots, below the soil line. Placing them at the leaves is a common misconception.
quiz.placement: Evidence mapping: placing resource cards on the maize diagram (green star = entry point)

quiz.prompt: A group places the carbon dioxide card on its maize diagram. Where does the maize plant take in carbon dioxide?
choices: Through the roots, together with the mineral salts
Through the stem, from the soil water
Through the leaves, from the air
Through the roots, from the soil
quiz.rationale: Carbon dioxide is a gas in the air. It enters the leaves through tiny openings called stomata, not the roots.
quiz.placement: Evidence mapping: placing resource cards on the maize diagram; ENTRY POINT | USE POINT table

quiz.prompt: Water enters a maize plant at the roots, but the leaves need it. Which statement best explains why the plant must have a transport system?
choices: Water is only needed in the roots, so a transport system is not needed
Water enters at one place and is needed at another, so something must carry it between them
The transport system is needed only to make the plant stand upright
Leaves can take in water directly from the air, so the roots are not important
quiz.rationale: The entry point (roots) and the use point (leaves) are different places. Something inside the plant must move the water from one to the other, and this is the transport system.
quiz.placement: Structured reasoning frame: 'Water enters the maize plant at the ____ ... the plant must have a ____'

quiz.prompt: The leaves of a maize plant make sugar using sunlight and carbon dioxide. The root cells also need sugar to stay alive. What must happen to the sugar?
choices: It stays in the leaf, because roots make their own sugar from soil water
It moves up from the roots to the leaf
It is carried from the leaf down through the stem to the roots
It is taken in from the soil by the roots, so no movement is needed
quiz.rationale: Sugar is made in the leaf, but the root also needs it. It must be transported down the stem, which is another reason a transport system is needed. Plants do not take in food from the soil.
quiz.placement: Structured reasoning frame extension: applying the same logic to sugars made in the leaf

quiz.prompt: Which statement about the Kibwezi maize is a correct cause-and-effect link, as a student might write on an orange sticky note?
choices: Mineral salts enter at the leaf, so the roots do not need to take in anything
Plants make food in the roots, so nothing needs to move through the stem
Water is in the soil, so the leaves always have enough water
Water enters at the root and is needed at the leaf, so the plant needs a transport system
quiz.rationale: Water entering at the root and being needed at the leaf shows why a transport system is necessary. The other statements repeat the misconceptions that water in the soil means water in the leaf, that mineral salts enter at the leaf, and that food is made in the roots.
quiz.placement: Driving Question Board: orange sticky note 'GROWING UNDERSTANDING' about the Kibwezi wilting maize

quiz.prompt: A farmer in Kibwezi waters her maize in the morning, yet the leaves wilt in the afternoon. The leaves are losing water faster than the plant's transport system can deliver it from the roots. What is the best conclusion?
choices: The plant wilts because there is no water in the soil
The plant can wilt even when the soil has water, because the leaves lose water faster than it is moved up from the roots
The plant wilts because mineral salts have entered at the leaves
The plant wilts because the leaves cannot make sugar
quiz.rationale: Water in the soil is not the same as water inside the leaf. If water is lost at the leaf faster than the transport system brings it from the root, the plant wilts.
quiz.placement: Whole-lesson revisit of the Kibwezi wilting maize; extension question and model sentence 'This model helps explain the Kibwezi wilting mystery because...'

lessons.title: The Big Picture: Overview of the Plant Transport System (Xylem and Phloem)

quiz.prompt: A farmer cuts across a maize stem and sees two different kinds of tubes. One kind carries water upward and the other carries something else. What are the two kinds of transport tubes in plants called?
choices: Phloem and stomata
Stomata and root hairs
Cortex and xylem
Xylem and phloem
quiz.rationale: Xylem and phloem are the two vascular tissues that transport materials in plants. Stomata and root hairs are other plant structures, and the cortex is a layer of root tissue, not a transport tube.
quiz.placement: Predict: scenario card and written predictions about the two types of tubes in the cut maize stem

quiz.prompt: In a maize plant, in which direction do water and mineral salts travel through the xylem?
choices: Upward from the soil through the root and stem to the leaves
From the leaves down to the roots
Only sideways from one leaf to another
In both directions equally, like a two-way road
quiz.rationale: Xylem carries water and mineral salts upward in one direction: soil, root, stem, then leaf. This is why the blue arrows on the diagram all point upward.
quiz.placement: Activity 2A: Whole-Plant Diagram Annotation (blue arrows for xylem)

quiz.prompt: A maize plant is growing a cob. The leaves make sugars by photosynthesis. Where does the phloem carry these manufactured food substances?
choices: From the leaves both downward to the roots and to the developing cob
Only upward from the roots to the leaves
From the soil to the leaves
Only downward to the roots, never to the cob
quiz.rationale: Phloem carries manufactured food from the leaves to places that need it, such as the roots and the developing cob. It is bidirectional but mainly downward. The belief that phloem only goes down is a common misconception.
quiz.placement: Activity 2A: Whole-Plant Diagram Annotation (red arrows for phloem, including the maize cob as a sink)

quiz.prompt: Which statement about xylem correctly compares it with phloem?
choices: Xylem carries water and mineral salts downward from the leaves.
Xylem carries sugars and is made of living cells.
Xylem and phloem carry exactly the same substances in the same direction.
Xylem carries water and mineral salts and is made of dead, hollow cells that form continuous tubes.
quiz.rationale: Xylem is made of dead, hollow cells with no nucleus that form continuous tubes carrying water and mineral salts upward. Sugars are carried by phloem, so the other statements mix up the two tissues.
quiz.placement: Activity 3A: Venn Diagram Compare & Contrast (type of cells, what is transported)

quiz.prompt: The xylem in a maize stem becomes blocked, so water cannot reach the leaves. What will most likely happen to the leaves?
choices: They will lose water from their cells, become less firm and droop (wilt).
They will make more food because the phloem works faster.
They will stay the same because the soil still has water.
They will grow firmer because they keep their sugars.
quiz.rationale: Blocked xylem means water cannot reach the leaf cells. The cells lose turgor, so the leaves droop and wilt. Water in the soil does not help if it cannot travel up the xylem.
quiz.placement: Activity 3C: Phenomenon Reconnect Discussion (what happens to the leaf if xylem is blocked)

quiz.prompt: A student writes this explanation for the wilting maize: 'Insufficient water reaching leaf cells via xylem → ______ → wilting.' Which phrase correctly fills the blank?
choices: Xylem carrying water downward
Roots growing too deep
Too much sugar in the phloem
Loss of turgor pressure in the leaf cells
quiz.rationale: When leaf cells do not get enough water, they lose turgor, meaning they are no longer firm like a well-filled balloon. This makes the leaf droop, which is wilting.
quiz.placement: Model v.1: thought-bubble explanation of wilting (xylem, water, turgor pressure, wilting)

quiz.prompt: A farmer in Kibwezi waters her maize soil in the morning, yet the plants wilt in the afternoon. Which statement shows the best understanding of the two transport tissues?
choices: Xylem carries water downward from the leaves to the soil, so the soil stays wet.
Watering the soil means the leaves must have enough water, so the wilting must be caused by phloem.
Water in the soil is carried to the leaves by the phloem, so the phloem must be blocked.
Water in the soil is not the same as water inside the plant. It must travel up the xylem to the leaf cells, and if it does not arrive fast enough the leaves lose turgor and wilt.
quiz.rationale: Water in the soil is only useful if it reaches the leaf cells through the xylem, which carries it upward. If supply to the leaves is too slow, the leaf cells lose turgor and the plant wilts, even when the soil is wet.
quiz.placement: End of lesson: reconnecting to the Kibwezi farmer's puzzle

lessons.title: The Entry Point: Root Structure and Water Absorption

quiz.prompt: A student looks at a maize seedling root with a hand lens and sees many tiny root hairs. Why are root hairs useful to the maize plant?
choices: They increase the surface area of the root for absorbing water and mineral salts
They store food for the seedling
They protect the root from insects and disease
They pump water up to the leaves
quiz.rationale: Each root hair is a long, thin extension of a root cell. Many root hairs greatly increase the surface area in contact with the soil, so more water and mineral salts can be absorbed.
quiz.placement: Part A: Root observation with hand lens (root hair drawing)

quiz.prompt: Two potato strips, each 5 cm long, are placed in a beaker of concentrated salt solution for 15 minutes. What is most likely to happen to them?
choices: They become shorter and floppy because water moves out of the potato cells into the salt solution
They stay exactly the same length and firmness
They become shorter only because the salt dissolves the potato
They become longer and firmer because they take in salt
quiz.rationale: The salt solution has a lower water potential than the potato cells, so water leaves the cells by osmosis. The strip loses water, becomes flaccid and shorter.
quiz.placement: Part B: Osmosis investigation with potato strips in tap water and concentrated salt solution

quiz.prompt: In the potato-strip investigation, all the strips are cut to the same starting length (about 5 cm). Why is this done?
choices: So that the strips will all absorb the same amount of salt
So that the strips will fit more easily into the beaker
So that any change in length can be fairly compared, because the only difference is the water or salt solution
So that the potato strips will not need to be measured again
quiz.rationale: Starting length is a controlled variable. Keeping it the same means that differences in final length are due to the liquid (tap water or salt solution) and not to the strips being different sizes.
quiz.placement: Part B: Osmosis investigation with potato strips (teacher demonstrates cutting a strip and asks why all strips must be equal length)

quiz.prompt: Which list shows the correct path taken by water as it enters a maize root from the soil?
choices: Xylem → endodermis → cortex → root hair cell
Root hair cell → endodermis → cortex → xylem
Cortex → root hair cell → xylem → endodermis
Root hair cell → cortex → endodermis → xylem
quiz.rationale: Water enters the root hair cell from the soil, crosses the cortex, passes through the endodermis, and finally reaches the xylem in the centre of the root.
quiz.placement: Whole-class explanation: building the root cross-section diagram and drawing arrows for water movement

quiz.prompt: The soil around a maize root has very few mineral salt ions, but the root hair cells contain many more of them. How do the mineral salts enter the root hair cells?
choices: By osmosis, in the same way as water
By simple diffusion from the soil into the root hair cell, with no energy needed
By active transport, using energy (ATP) from respiration in the root cells
By being pulled in through the Casparian strip without passing through any cell
quiz.rationale: The salts move from low concentration (soil) to high concentration (cell), against the concentration gradient. This needs active transport, which uses ATP from respiration. Osmosis and diffusion only move substances down a gradient.
quiz.placement: Whole-class explanation: mineral salts and active transport (where does the energy come from?)

quiz.prompt: The endodermis of a root has a waxy band called the Casparian strip. What does it do?
choices: It absorbs water directly from the soil into the xylem
It forces water to pass through living cells, so the plant can control what gets into the xylem
It makes mineral salts move by osmosis instead of active transport
It stores extra water for the plant during the dry season
quiz.rationale: The waxy Casparian strip blocks the gaps between endodermis cells. Water must therefore pass through the living cells, which acts as a checkpoint for what enters the xylem.
quiz.placement: Whole-class explanation: Casparian strip in the endodermis (a checkpoint)

quiz.prompt: A farmer in Kibwezi waters her maize in the morning with very salty irrigation water. By afternoon the plants are wilting, even though the soil is wet. Which is the best explanation?
choices: The soil water has a higher water potential than the root hair cells, so water moves in too fast and the plant wilts
The roots cannot use salty water because mineral salts only enter by osmosis
The wet soil is blocking oxygen, so the root hairs have grown too long
The soil water now has a lower water potential than the root hair cells, so water cannot enter by osmosis and may even leave the root
quiz.rationale: Salt lowers the water potential of the soil water. If it falls below that of the root hair cells, osmosis stops or reverses, so the plant loses water and wilts even though water is present, as the potato strip in salt solution showed.
quiz.placement: DQB update: 'Why does the Kibwezi farmer's maize wilt even when the soil has water?' (green sticky-note answers)

lessons.title: The Highway: Stem Structure and Vascular Bundles

quiz.prompt: Your group cuts a cross-section of a fresh bean stem to look at under a hand lens. Why must the section be cut as thinly as possible?
choices: So that the stain can change xylem into phloem
So that light can pass through it and the tissues can be seen clearly
So that the vascular bundles are removed and only the pith is seen
So that the stem stays alive for longer after cutting
quiz.rationale: A thin section lets light pass through, so the stained regions and bundles can be seen and drawn. A thick section hides the detail.
quiz.placement: Step 1: cutting thin cross-sections of the bean or sunflower stem

quiz.prompt: A group cuts and stains a bean stem and a maize stem. Which description of the vascular bundles is correct?
choices: Both stems have vascular bundles scattered through the stem
The bean stem has bundles in a ring, and the maize stem has bundles scattered through the stem
The bean stem has bundles scattered, and the maize stem has bundles in a ring
Both stems have vascular bundles arranged in a ring
quiz.rationale: The dicot (bean or sunflower) stem has its bundles in a ring. The monocot (maize) stem has its bundles scattered.
quiz.placement: Kenya context: cutting, staining and sketching the maize stem and comparing it with the bean stem

quiz.prompt: A student looks at a stained stem section through a hand lens. Which statement is an OBSERVATION (what I see) and not an inference (what I think it is)?
choices: The patches are the highway that the Kibwezi maize needs
The cells in the dark patches are dead
The stained patches carry water up to the leaves
The dark patches form a ring near the outside of the stem
quiz.rationale: Describing the colour and arrangement of patches is something you can see directly. The other statements explain what the patches are or what they do, so they are inferences.
quiz.placement: Step 3: drawing the cross-section and separating 'What I See' from 'What I Think It Is'

quiz.prompt: Which description of xylem is correct?
choices: Dead, thick-walled tubes that carry water and mineral salts upward
Dead, thin-walled cells that store food in the pith
Living cells with companion cells that carry water downward
Living cells with thin walls that carry sugars downward
quiz.rationale: Xylem is made of dead cells with thick walls, forming tubes that carry water and mineral salts upward from the roots. Living thin-walled tissue with sugar transport describes phloem.
quiz.placement: Jigsaw expert Group A (xylem experts): structure, wall thickness, dead cells and role in water transport

quiz.prompt: A student says: 'Phloem is just another tube like xylem, so it also carries water up to the leaves.' Which statement correctly describes phloem?
choices: It supports the stem because its walls are very thick
It is made of dead cells and carries water only upward
It is made of living sieve tubes with companion cells and carries sugars made in the leaves, mainly downward
It stores water in the cortex of the root
quiz.rationale: Phloem is living tissue made of sieve tubes and companion cells. It carries manufactured food (sugars) from the leaves to other parts of the plant, mainly downward.
quiz.placement: Jigsaw expert Group B (phloem experts): sieve tubes, companion cells and role in sugar transport

quiz.prompt: In one vascular bundle of a bean stem cross-section, which arrangement of xylem and phloem is correct?
choices: Both are found only in the pith
Xylem towards the centre (pith side) and phloem towards the outside (epidermis side)
Xylem towards the outside (epidermis side) and phloem towards the centre (pith side)
Xylem and phloem are mixed together with no pattern
quiz.rationale: In each bundle the xylem lies on the inner side, towards the pith, and the phloem lies on the outer side, towards the epidermis.
quiz.placement: Adding the stem layer to the cumulative transport model: labelling xylem and phloem in a vascular bundle

quiz.prompt: A farmer in Kibwezi waters her maize in the morning, but the plants still wilt and some die. The soil is wet. Which explanation fits what you have learnt about stem structure?
choices: If the xylem in the stem is blocked, for example by air bubbles, or the roots are destroyed, water cannot reach the leaves even though the soil is wet
The vascular bundles in maize are scattered, so they cannot carry any water
Wet soil always gives enough water, so the wilting must be caused by the phloem carrying too much sugar down
Xylem carries sugars to the roots, so watering the soil makes no difference
quiz.rationale: Water must travel up through the xylem to reach the leaves. If the xylem is blocked or the roots are damaged, the highway is broken and the plant wilts permanently even when the soil has water.
quiz.placement: Jigsaw expert Group D and Connect-Back: what could break the highway in the Kibwezi maize?

lessons.title: The Destination: Leaf Structure and Transpiration

quiz.prompt: Before school, a clear polythene bag was tied tightly around a leafy branch of a Ficus tree. By mid-morning, water droplets were seen on the inside of the bag. Where did this water mainly come from?
choices: Water that dripped from the soil up the outside of the branch
Water vapour lost by the leaves, which condensed on the inside of the bag
Water that came through tiny holes in the polythene bag
Rain that condensed on the outside of the bag and leaked in
quiz.rationale: The leaves lose water vapour (transpiration), and it cools and condenses on the inside of the bag. The bag was sealed and kept off the soil, so rain or leaking cannot explain the water.
quiz.placement: Predict: the 'sweating leaf bag' observation and Think–Pair–Share prediction

quiz.prompt: A celery stalk was left standing in red food dye for several hours. When a cross-section was cut, only small dots in the stalk were stained red. What does this show?
choices: The dye moved through the outer skin of the stalk, so the skin carries water
Phloem carries water up the stem, so phloem is stained
The dye moved through xylem tissue, so xylem carries water up the stem
The dye moved through all the cells equally, so all cells carry water up the stem
quiz.rationale: Only the xylem was stained, so the dye travelled in the xylem. This confirms that xylem carries water from the roots up the stem to the leaves.
quiz.placement: Observation A: dye experiment results (celery stalks from Lesson 5)

quiz.prompt: A learner makes stomatal impressions with clear nail varnish from the upper and lower surfaces of a sukuma wiki leaf and counts the stomata under a microscope. Which result is normally expected?
choices: More stomata on the lower surface than on the upper surface
More stomata on the upper surface than on the lower surface
Exactly the same number of stomata on both surfaces
No stomata on either surface, because stomata are found only in the roots
quiz.rationale: Most leaves such as sukuma wiki have more stomata on the lower surface, which is usually shaded and loses less water. If the counts are equal or reversed, the learner may have applied varnish to the wrong side.
quiz.placement: Observation B: stomatal impression practical (upper vs lower surface counts)

quiz.prompt: The upper surface of a sukuma wiki leaf feels slightly waxy and shiny. What is the main job of this waxy cuticle?
choices: To let water vapour escape quickly from the leaf
To absorb water from the air into the leaf
To reduce water loss from the leaf surface
To carry water from the roots into the leaf
quiz.rationale: The waxy cuticle is waterproof and reduces water loss through the epidermis. Most water vapour therefore leaves through the stomata, not through the cuticle.
quiz.placement: Observation C: leaf cross-section and waxy cuticle of the upper surface

quiz.prompt: At 2:00 pm in Kibwezi it is 38°C, windy and very dry. A farmer watered her maize in the morning, yet the maize is wilting. Which explanation is correct?
choices: The soil has no water left, so the roots have nothing to absorb
The wind blows water into the leaves, which makes them heavy and droop
Water is lost through the stomata faster than the roots and xylem can replace it
The plants are thirsty because the xylem has stopped carrying water
quiz.rationale: High temperature, strong wind and low humidity increase the rate of transpiration. When water is lost through the stomata faster than it is taken up, the leaves lose turgor and the plant wilts, even if the soil still has water.
quiz.placement: Explain: Kibwezi group explanation (2:00 pm, 38°C, strong wind, very low humidity)

quiz.prompt: A sukuma wiki plot shaded by a large mango tree barely wilts, while maize in the open field wilts badly. Which is the best explanation?
choices: The mango tree gives its water to the sukuma wiki through the roots
Sukuma wiki has no stomata, so it cannot lose water
Shade makes the air drier, so the sukuma wiki loses less water
Shade lowers light intensity and temperature, so the sukuma wiki loses water more slowly
quiz.rationale: Shade reduces light and temperature around the leaves, which lowers the rate of transpiration. Sukuma wiki does have stomata, and drier air would increase water loss, not reduce it.
quiz.placement: Explain: factors affecting transpiration table (sheltered sukuma wiki under mango tree vs open maize field)

quiz.prompt: Which order correctly shows the journey of water from the soil to the atmosphere through a maize plant?
choices: Soil → root hair → phloem → leaf mesophyll → cuticle → atmosphere
Soil → root hair → xylem → leaf mesophyll → stomata → atmosphere
Soil → leaf mesophyll → xylem → root hair → stomata → atmosphere
Soil → stem xylem → root hair → stomata → leaf mesophyll → atmosphere
quiz.rationale: Water enters the root hairs by osmosis, travels up the xylem to the leaf, moves into the mesophyll cells and leaves as water vapour through the stomata into the atmosphere.
quiz.placement: DQB: board timeline Soil → Root → Stem → Leaf → ATMOSPHERE

quiz.prompt: A learner adds an arrow to her plant model to show transpiration. Which arrow and label is correct?
choices: From the waxy cuticle outward, labelled 'most water vapour exits'
From the xylem to the roots, labelled 'water vapour exits'
From the soil into the root hairs, labelled 'transpiration'
From the stomata outward, labelled 'water vapour exits'
quiz.rationale: Transpiration is the loss of water vapour from a plant, mainly through the stomata of the leaves. The arrow must therefore leave through the stomata, not the cuticle, and not at the roots.
quiz.placement: Model: adding the 'water vapour exits as transpiration' arrow to the cumulative transport model

lessons.title: The Engine: Transpiration Pull, Cohesion-Tension, and Root Pressure

quiz.prompt: A farmer in Kibwezi has a maize plant 3 metres tall. Which statement best explains what pulls water from the soil to the top leaf?
choices: The roots push all the water up the stem, and this push is strongest at 2 pm.
Capillarity alone lifts the water the full 3 metres, because it creeps up narrow tubes.
Gravity pulls water upward through the xylem when the sun is hot.
Evaporation of water from the leaves pulls the water column up the xylem.
quiz.rationale: Water evaporating from the leaves through the stomata (transpiration) lowers water potential in the leaf and pulls the water column upward. Capillarity lifts water well under a metre, and root pressure only supplements this.
quiz.placement: Predict: tall maize diagram Think-Pair-Share with PUSHING and PULLING columns

quiz.prompt: In a potometer investigation, a lamp was directed at the leaves of a shoot. The air bubble in the capillary tube moved 27 mm in 6 minutes. What was the water uptake rate?
choices: 4.5 mm/min
27 mm/min
162 mm/min
0.2 mm/min
quiz.rationale: Rate = distance ÷ time = 27 mm ÷ 6 min = 4.5 mm/min. Giving only the distance, or multiplying instead of dividing, are common errors.
quiz.placement: Part: potometer investigation, calculating average rate (mm/min) for each condition

quiz.prompt: In a potometer investigation, a group covered both surfaces of all the leaves with petroleum jelly. The bubble moved much more slowly than in the control. What is the best explanation?
choices: The petroleum jelly increased root pressure, which pushed the bubble backwards.
The petroleum jelly blocked the stomata, so less water was lost by transpiration and less water was pulled up the stem.
The petroleum jelly made the xylem vessels wider, so the water slowed down.
The petroleum jelly made the water molecules stop sticking together.
quiz.rationale: Blocked stomata reduce water loss from the leaf. This weakens the transpiration pull and so reduces the rate at which the stem takes up water.
quiz.placement: Part: potometer investigation, Condition D (petroleum jelly on the leaves) and class bar graph

quiz.prompt: Which property of water molecules allows the pull from transpiration at the leaf to move the whole water column in the xylem, right down to the roots?
choices: Water molecules change into gas inside the xylem vessels.
Water molecules stick together through hydrogen bonds (cohesion), so the column moves like a chain.
Water molecules are pumped up by the xylem walls using energy.
Water molecules repel each other, so they spread out along the xylem.
quiz.rationale: Cohesion, the sticking together of water molecules by hydrogen bonds, lets a pull at the top move the whole column. This is the cohesion-tension mechanism, like students holding hands in a line.
quiz.placement: Explain: guided cohesion-tension diagram and the chain-of-students analogy

quiz.prompt: Which statement about root pressure is correct?
choices: It is the main force lifting water on a hot, windy afternoon when the stomata are wide open.
It is a pulling force produced by evaporation at the leaf.
It is a supplementary push: roots take up mineral ions, water enters by osmosis, and water can be forced upward, as seen in guttation.
It is the force that lets capillarity lift water 3 metres.
quiz.rationale: Active uptake of ions lowers the water potential of root cells, so water enters by osmosis and can push water up, especially at night or in moist conditions. It supplements transpiration pull and does not replace it.
quiz.placement: Explain: teacher's brief explanation of root pressure and guttation

quiz.prompt: A farmer in Kibwezi waters her maize in the morning, yet it wilts at 2 pm on a hot, windy afternoon. Which explanation is best?
choices: Water is lost by transpiration faster than the roots can absorb it, so the plant loses water faster than it gains it, even though the soil is wet.
Water moves down the xylem in the afternoon, so the leaves get no water.
The soil water has disappeared completely, so there is nothing for the roots to absorb.
The roots push too much water into the plant, which makes the leaves collapse.
quiz.rationale: Heat and wind raise the transpiration rate, which strengthens the pull. If the rate of absorption cannot keep up with the rate of water loss, the plant wilts even when the soil contains water.
quiz.placement: DQB: sticky note answering 'Why does the Kibwezi maize wilt even when the farmer has already watered the soil?'

quiz.prompt: A student is adding the Lesson 7 'engine' to a plant transport model. Which addition is correct?
choices: A transpiration label at the root, because the pull starts where water enters the plant.
Arrows in the xylem pointing downward from leaf to root, because water is pulled by gravity.
A root pressure label showing it as the main driver of water movement on a hot afternoon.
Arrows in the xylem pointing upward from root to leaf, with a label at the stomata saying that transpiration creates tension that pulls the water column up.
quiz.rationale: The pull starts at the top of the chain, at the leaf, where transpiration through the stomata creates tension. Cohesion-tension arrows therefore point upward, and root pressure is only supplementary.
quiz.placement: Model: adding cohesion-tension arrows, transpiration label and root pressure label to the cumulative transport model

lessons.title: The Return Journey: Translocation and Final Model Build

quiz.prompt: A ring of bark, including the phloem, is cut all the way round the trunk of a mango tree (girdling). After some weeks the roots below the cut start to die. Which is the best explanation?
choices: The roots cannot get water because the bark carries water up from the soil
The roots make their own sugar, and this stops when the bark is cut
The roots are damaged by too much sunlight after the bark is removed
The roots cannot get sugars made in the leaves because the phloem that carries them down has been cut
quiz.rationale: Phloem carries sucrose made in the leaves (source) down to the roots (sink). A complete ring cut blocks this, so the roots starve and die.
quiz.placement: Activity A: Girdling Evidence Analysis

quiz.prompt: In a girdled bean plant, after 48 hours the sucrose concentration was 4.2% above the girdle and 0.3% below the girdle. What does this data show?
choices: Sugar travels down the plant in the bark (phloem) from the leaves, and the girdle stopped it at the cut
Sugar cannot move through any part of a plant
Sugar travels in the xylem along with water, and the girdle slowed the water down
Sugar is made in the roots and travels upwards in the xylem
quiz.rationale: Sucrose built up above the cut and was low below it. This shows the tissue that was removed, the phloem, normally carries sugar downward from the leaves.
quiz.placement: Activity A: Girdling Evidence Analysis (sucrose data table)

quiz.prompt: In a model of the pressure-flow hypothesis, Beaker A holds concentrated sucrose solution and Beaker B holds dilute sucrose solution. Each is separated from a water reservoir by a semi-permeable membrane, and the two are joined by a glass tube. The red solution is seen to move along the tube from A towards B. Why does it move?
choices: The solution moves because the water in Beaker B evaporates
Sucrose molecules are pulled through the tube by gravity
The solution moves because the membrane pumps sucrose into the tube
Water enters Beaker A by osmosis, which builds pressure that pushes the solution along the tube towards B
quiz.rationale: The concentrated solution in A draws in water by osmosis. This raises the pressure in A, and the higher pressure pushes the solution towards the lower-pressure end (B).
quiz.placement: Activity B: Pressure-Flow Model Demonstration

quiz.prompt: In the pressure-flow hypothesis, what happens at a sink, such as a root cell or a maize cob, that helps keep sugars flowing towards it?
choices: Water is pulled up from the sink by transpiration, which pushes sugar away
Sucrose is unloaded and used, and water leaves the phloem by osmosis, so the pressure falls
Sucrose is loaded into the phloem and water enters by osmosis, so the pressure rises
Sucrose is made by photosynthesis, which raises the pressure
quiz.rationale: At the sink, sucrose is unloaded and used and water leaves the sieve tube by osmosis, so pressure is lower than at the source. The pressure gradient drives mass flow from source to sink.
quiz.placement: Part A: Direct Instruction Consolidation (pressure-flow steps)

quiz.prompt: Which statement correctly compares xylem and phloem in a maize plant?
choices: Xylem and phloem both carry water and sugar in both directions
Xylem carries water and mineral salts from the roots to the leaves by transpiration pull, and phloem carries sucrose and amino acids from source to sink by pressure flow
Xylem carries sucrose and amino acids from source to sink by pressure flow, and phloem carries water up by transpiration pull
Xylem is made of living sieve tubes, and phloem is made of dead hollow vessels
quiz.rationale: Xylem moves water and mineral salts upwards, driven by transpiration pull (cohesion-tension), through dead vessels. Phloem moves sucrose and amino acids from source to sink by pressure flow, through living sieve tubes.
quiz.placement: Part B: Compare and Contrast (xylem and phloem T-table)

quiz.prompt: On a hot, dry afternoon in Kibwezi, two maize plants both wilt. By morning one has recovered but the other has died. Which explanation best fits the plant that did NOT recover?
choices: A severe, long water deficit made the tension in the xylem so large that air entered and broke the water columns, so water could no longer move up
The roots had too much sugar from the leaves
It was thirsty, and thirst alone is enough to kill a plant
The phloem carried all the water down to the roots, so none reached the leaves
quiz.rationale: When water loss is severe and long, the tension in the xylem can break the water columns (cavitation) and damage cells. The plant then cannot move water upward even if it is watered again. Plants with unbroken columns recover when it cools in the evening.
quiz.placement: Part C: Connecting to Kibwezi (Why do some plants die while others recover?)

quiz.prompt: A sukuma wiki plot shaded by a mango tree barely wilts, while maize in full sun nearby wilts badly. Which is the best explanation?
choices: Shade makes the phloem carry water instead of sugar
Shade makes the soil produce more water than the roots need
Shade lowers light and temperature, so less water is lost by transpiration and the leaf cells keep their turgor
Shade stops the roots from taking in any water
quiz.rationale: In shade, light and temperature are lower, so stomata lose less water by transpiration. The xylem tension stays lower and the cells stay turgid, so the plants do not wilt.
quiz.placement: Part C: Connecting to Kibwezi (Why does the sukuma wiki under the mango tree barely wilt?)
